_comment: The hooks below are the office floor's only source of truth. Every one of them is
read-only observability — none returns a decision, none can block a tool call.
Enforcement (who may delegate, budget ceilings) lives in the app, not here.
_permissions_comment: What the office may do without being asked.
This list is not convenience. The office runs on `claude -p`, which has no way to answer
a permission prompt: anything not pre-authorised is simply refused, and the agent finds
out by being told no. `acceptEdits` covers reading and writing files, so an office
without this block can write code all day and cannot run a single test.
That is not a papercut. The second standing order is that claims are verified, not
believed, and every task carries a VERIFY condition — which is a command. An office that
cannot run commands cannot verify anything, so its central rule quietly becomes a wish.
The shape of the list: everything here either inspects without changing anything, or is
one of this project's own verification commands. Nothing here reaches the network,
deletes anything, or publishes anything. Adding your project's test command is expected;
widening it to `Bash(*)` is not — at that point you have `bypassPermissions` with extra
steps, and `docs/running.md` already tells you how to ask for that on purpose.
Why `curl` is not on either list.
It was denied outright, which also blocked `curl localhost:3000` — and hitting its own dev
server is the only way the office can prove the thing it just built actually serves. With
`node -e` denied too (rightly: an interpreter with an inline-code flag walks past every rule
here), both routes to 'is it responding?' were shut, so an office could build a site and
never verify it.
`curl localhost` cannot be allowed on its own: rules match by prefix and the `:` in
`localhost:3000` collides with the `:*` wildcard, so no narrower rule matches anything. That
was measured against ruleCovers, not assumed.
So curl is unlisted, which is neither yes nor no: it becomes an approval card naming the
exact command, and you decide. A local check is one click; anything reaching off this
machine is visible before it happens rather than silently refused. Same treatment as `npx`
and `pip install`, and for the same reason.
_hooks_comment: The approval gate, registered. Until 2026-08-20 this block was {} and the comment here said
the gate would go in 'when approvals are built (J-4)'. Approvals had been built: the hook, the
133 lines in approvals.ts that wait on it, and a panel. Nothing registered it, so PreToolUse
never ran, so no request was ever written, so the app watched an empty directory - with a
green test suite throughout. CLAUDE.md meanwhile told every agent the gate 'can refuse a tool
call'. It could not. test/repo-health.test.ts now fails if a hook file is never registered.
Why the matcher is Bash and not '*'. Bash is the tool the permission lists above are about;
Read and Grep change nothing, and Write/Edit are what acceptEdits exists to cover. Gating
everything would ask a person about reading a file.
Why this does not stall the verify harness: verify.ts spawns VERIFY commands itself, through
child_process, never through the CLI. They do not pass this hook at all.
Why it does not ask about `npm test`: measured - PreToolUse fires before permission
resolution, so an allow-listed command reaches the hook anyway. approvals.ts triages every
request against the policy above before a person sees it: allowed answers itself, denied
answers itself with the rule, and only *unlisted* becomes a question. That is the case the
gate is for - `claude --print` cannot stop and ask, so an unlisted command is simply refused
today, and the employee finds out by being told no.
timeout 300 against the hook's own 240s wait, so it answers rather than being killed
mid-decision. An unanswered request is a denial and the hook enforces that itself.
